entries.value: The plain of Marathon, 490 BC
This act restores that defense. Hold one road, learn what a line costs, and finish standing.

Darius of Persia sent a fleet west to punish Athens for backing the Ionian revolt. It beached at Marathon, one day's march from the city. Athens went out with Plataea beside her and no Spartan column in sight, because Sparta was keeping a religious festival and would arrive after the fighting ended. Miltiades thinned his centre, weighted both wings, let the Persian middle push forward, and closed on it from either side. Herodotus counted 192 Athenian dead. The same men then walked forty kilometres home in armour to meet the fleet before it could reach an undefended city.
Attican Boot Sequence
The Delian League, founded 478 BC
This act restores the alliance. Many islands, many roads, and the slow discovery that protection and control wear the same face.

With Persia thrown back, the island states swore a common alliance and put its treasury on Delos, the birthplace of Apollo, where by sacred law no one was allowed to be born or to die. Members paid in ships or in silver. It held until Naxos tried to leave: the alliance besieged it, took its walls and its fleet, and Thucydides marked that as the first ally reduced to a subject, against everything the league had sworn. The treasury moved to Athens in 454 BC.
Shards of the Aegean
The Hot Gates and Delphi, 480 BC
This act restores the narrow ground and the ambiguous answer. Fewer places to stand, and a prophecy worth only as much as your reading of it.

Xerxes returned with an army the Greeks could not meet in open country, so they chose ground where numbers could not spread out. Thermopylae was a coastal pass only a few paces wide, and Leonidas held it for two days. On the third a local man named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain track around it. Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with his Spartans, the Thespians who refused to leave, and the Thebans. At the same time Delphi told Athens to trust a wooden wall. The priests meant the palisade on the Acropolis. Themistocles argued it meant the fleet, and the fleet won at Salamis.
Oracle War
The Peloponnesian War, 431 to 404 BC
This act restores the last defense, the one fought against something the network built itself.

The alliance that saved Greece from Persia turned on itself. Athens and Sparta fought for twenty-seven years. Plague took perhaps a third of the city from behind its own walls, and Pericles with it. The fleet that had won at Salamis was thrown away in Sicily. Athens surrendered in 404 BC and the long walls came down to the sound of flutes. No foreign power ended the golden age. It was ended from the inside, by people certain they were defending it.
